title: THE DANGEROUS PRAYER OF SAMSON
paragraphs: THE DANGEROUS PRAYER OF SAMSON
There are prayers that sound holy but are secretly selfish.
Prayers that ask God to bless our plans.
Prayers that ask Him to protect our comfort.
Prayers that ask Him to remove consequences while allowing us to keep our idols.
Then there are prayers so dangerous that they can only be prayed by someone who has finally run out of excuses.
Samson prayed one of those prayers.
His final prayer was not spoken from a place of strength.
It was spoken from humiliation.
From failure.
From regret.
From a prison cell.
From a life that had become the very opposite of what God intended.
And that is precisely why it still speaks to us today.
Because many people know the God of Samson's victories.
Far fewer understand the God who met Samson in his lowest moment.
Far fewer understand that some of the most powerful prayers in Scripture were not prayed by heroes standing tall.
They were prayed by broken people lying in the dust.
The story begins long before the prison.
Long before the chains.
Long before the blindness.
Long before Delilah.
Samson's life was surrounded by divine purpose from the beginning.
The angel of the LORD announced his birth before he was conceived.
Judges 13 presents a child set apart by God for a holy purpose.
He was to be a Nazirite.
The Hebrew word is נָזִיר (Nazir), meaning "one consecrated" or "one separated unto God."
Samson was not called because he was strong.
He was strong because he was called.
That distinction matters.
Many believers today mistakenly believe their gifting is their identity.
But gifts are not identity.
Calling is.
Strength is not identity.
Christ is.
Samson spent much of his life confusing God's power with God's approval.
And many Christians still do the same.
They assume that because God is using them, God must be pleased with them.
But gifting can continue operating long after intimacy has faded.
Ministry success can hide spiritual decay.
Public victories can conceal private compromise.
Samson's life became a slow-motion scandal.
One compromise after another.
One rationalization after another.
One temptation after another.
Until eventually his heart drifted far from the God who had called him.
The tragedy of Samson was not merely that he fell.
The tragedy was that he believed he could keep playing with sin indefinitely.
Judges 16 records the devastating moment.
Delilah pressed him daily.
His resistance weakened.
His discernment faded.
His pride grew.
Eventually he revealed the secret associated with his Nazirite vow.
Then came one of the saddest verses in all of Scripture:
"He did not know that the LORD had left him."
The Hebrew text says:
וְהוּא לֹא יָדַע כִּי יְהוָה סָר מֵעָלָיו
(vehu lo yada ki Yahweh sar me'alav)
"He did not know that Yahweh had departed from him."
Judges 16:20
Notice what the text does not say.
It does not say God stopped existing.
It does not say God's covenant promises disappeared.
It does not say God's mercy ended.
It says Samson no longer recognized what had changed.
That is one of the greatest dangers in the Christian life.
Spiritual drift rarely feels dramatic.
It feels normal.
It feels gradual.
Until one day we realize we have been relying on yesterday's intimacy while living far from today's obedience.
The Philistines captured him.
They gouged out his eyes.
They chained him.
They forced him into slavery.
The mighty warrior became a public spectacle.
The man who once shattered armies could no longer see the hand in front of his face.
Everything he trusted was gone.
His strength.
His freedom.
His reputation.
His future.
His dignity.
And perhaps for the first time in his life, Samson was finally in a position where God had his full attention.
Many of us spend years asking God to make us stronger.
But sometimes God allows weakness because weakness accomplishes what strength never could.
The Apostle Paul later discovered this same truth.
The Greek text of 2 Corinthians 12:9 says:
ἡ γὰρ δύναμίς μου ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
(hē gar dynamis mou en astheneia teleitai)
"My power is perfected in weakness."
The Kingdom of God operates differently than the kingdoms of men.
God often does His deepest work after our self-confidence collapses.
After our masks break.
After our pretending ends.
After our scandals expose what pride was hiding.
The world sees failure as the end.
The Gospel often reveals it as the beginning.
Then comes Samson's final prayer.
One of the most overlooked prayers in all Scripture.
Judges 16:28 says:
"Then Samson called to the LORD and said, 'O Lord GOD, remember me, I pray. Strengthen me, I pray, only this once, O God.'"
The Hebrew begins:
זָכְרֵנִי נָא
(zakreni na)
"Remember me, please."
Not because God had forgotten him.
Biblical remembrance is covenant language.
It is an appeal to God's mercy.
An appeal to God's faithfulness.
An appeal to grace.
Samson is no longer bargaining.
No longer boasting.
No longer trusting himself.
The man who once acted as though he needed no one is now desperately dependent upon God.
That is the dangerous prayer.
"Remember me."
Not because I deserve it.
Not because I earned it.
Not because I have been faithful.
But because You are faithful.
That prayer still terrifies pride.
Because pride wants merit.
Grace offers mercy.
Pride wants achievement.
Grace offers redemption.
Pride says, "Look what I have done."
Grace says, "Look what Christ has done."
Samson's greatest victory did not happen when he carried city gates.
It did not happen when he defeated a thousand men.
It happened when he finally surrendered.
The final scene is shocking.
The blind prisoner stands between two pillars.
The crowd mocks.
The enemies celebrate.
Then God answers.
The building collapses.
The oppressors fall.
And Scripture says Samson accomplished more in his death than during much of his life.
This does not glorify Samson.
It glorifies God.
Because the story was never ultimately about Samson's strength.
It was about God's mercy.
That is the thread woven through the entire Bible.
Abraham lied.
Jacob deceived.
Moses murdered.
David committed adultery.
Peter denied Christ.
Yet God continued writing.
Because God specializes in redemption stories.
The Gospel reaches its highest expression at the cross.
Humanity's greatest scandal became Heaven's greatest display of grace.
The cross looked like defeat.
It became victory.
It looked like shame.
It became glory.
It looked like the end.
It became the beginning.
Jesus Himself cried out in Aramaic:
אֵלִי אֵלִי לְמָה שְׁבַקְתַּנִי
(Eli, Eli, lema shevaqtani)
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?"
Matthew 27:46
The sinless Son entered the place sinners deserved so sinners could receive the grace they never deserved.
Samson points us forward to Someone greater.
A Deliverer who would not fail.
A Judge who would never compromise.
A Savior who would not need redemption Himself.
Jesus Christ.
And perhaps that is why Samson's prayer still matters.
Because many people reading this know exactly what it feels like to sit in the ruins of their own decisions.
Some have lost marriages.
Some have lost ministries.
Some have lost opportunities.
Some have lost years.
Some have lost faith in themselves.
You may feel as though your story has become a scandal.
You may believe the damage is irreversible.
You may wonder whether God can still use someone who has failed so badly.
Samson's final prayer answers that question.
Yes.
Not because your failure is small.
But because God's mercy is bigger.
The enemy wants you convinced that your worst chapter defines you.
Jesus says otherwise.
The Gospel declares that repentance is never wasted.
Grace is never exhausted.
Mercy is never depleted.
And redemption is never beyond reach.
Be honest.
This hit harder than you expected.
Someone you love desperately needs this reminder today.
If this ministry has strengthened your faith, encouraged your walk, or pointed you closer to Jesus, your support becomes part of that mission.
Because sometimes the most dangerous prayer is not, "Lord make me stronger."
Sometimes it is, "Lord, after everything I have done, remember me."
And that is exactly where grace begins.
The chapter that embarrassed you may become the chapter that introduces people to the mercy of God.
